t2.newton:
*When:* The motion of an object is set by the forces on it, or you must find a force from a given motion.

*Why:* Acceleration comes from the net force, not from any single force. With zero net force the velocity stays constant, so no force is needed to keep a body moving.

*Move:*
$$\sum\vec F=m\vec a$$
Isolate one object. Add the forces on it as vectors. Write one equation per axis. For touching bodies, treat them as one system to find $a$, then isolate one body for the contact force. For every force a pair exists, equal and opposite, but it acts on the other body.

*Example:* A $5.0$ kg body feels $3.0$ N along $+x$ and $4.0$ N along $+y$.
$$a_x=\frac{3.0}{5.0}=0.60,\quad a_y=\frac{4.0}{5.0}=0.80\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$$
$$a=\sqrt{0.60^{2}+0.80^{2}}=1.0\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$$

*Trap:* Cancelling an action-reaction pair, which acts on two different bodies, or using one force instead of the net force.

*Check:* The acceleration points along the net force, and doubling the mass halves it.
t2.fbd:
*When:* Any problem with forces on a body, whether it sits still or accelerates.

*Why:* Most errors are a missing force or a force that does not exist. A diagram forces you to list each real force once, with its direction.

*Move:*
$$\sum F_x=ma_x,\qquad \sum F_y=ma_y$$
Choose one body. Draw weight $mg$ down, the normal force perpendicular to the surface, tension along the rope, and friction along the surface. Pick axes with one along the acceleration.

*Example:* A $6.0$ kg block on a table is pulled by a rope with $25$ N at $37^\circ$ above horizontal. It stays on the table.
$$N+T\sin37^\circ-mg=0$$
$$N=(6.0)(9.8)-(25)(0.60)=44\ \mathrm N$$

*Trap:* Drawing a force of motion, or assuming the normal force always equals $mg$.

*Check:* The normal force cannot be negative. A negative value means the body has left the surface.
t2.friction-drag:
*When:* A body touches a surface, or moves through air or liquid.

*Why:* Static friction adjusts to whatever is needed, up to a limit. Once sliding, kinetic friction has a fixed size. Drag grows with speed until it balances the weight.

*Move:*
$$f_s\le\mu_sN,\qquad f_k=\mu_kN,\qquad mg=bv_t\ \text{(linear drag)}$$
First compare the applied force with the limit $\mu_sN$. If it is smaller, friction equals the applied force and nothing moves. If larger, use $\mu_kN$ against the motion.

*Example:* A $20$ kg box has $\mu_s=0.45$ and $\mu_k=0.35$. A $100$ N push is applied. Here $N=mg=196$ N.
$$\mu_sN=0.45(196)=88\ \mathrm N<100\ \mathrm N\ \Rightarrow\ \text{slides}$$
$$a=\frac{100-0.35(196)}{20}=1.6\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$$

*Trap:* Using $\mu_sN$ as the friction force before the body slips.

*Check:* Friction opposes the relative motion, and the box accelerates only if the push beats the limit.
t2.incline-pulley:
*When:* A block sits on a slope, or masses hang over a pulley on a rope.

*Why:* On a slope, gravity splits into a part along the surface and a part into it. On a pulley, the rope links the accelerations and carries one tension.

*Move:*
$$a=g\sin\theta-\mu g\cos\theta,\qquad N=mg\cos\theta$$
$$a=\frac{(m_1-m_2)g}{m_1+m_2}\quad\text{(Atwood machine)}$$
Tilt the axes: one along the slope, one perpendicular. For a pulley, write $\sum F=ma$ for each mass and use the same tension for a massless frictionless pulley.

*Example:* A block slides down a $37^\circ$ slope with $\mu_k=0.25$.
$$a=9.8\,(\sin37^\circ-0.25\cos37^\circ)=9.8\,(0.60-0.20)\approx3.9\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$$

*Trap:* Using cosine for the part along the slope, or giving each side of the pulley its own tension.

*Check:* With no friction the result is $g\sin\theta$. Friction only lowers it.
t2.circular:
*When:* A body follows a curved path at steady speed, such as a car on a bend or a satellite.

*Why:* A changing direction means acceleration toward the centre. Some real force must supply it, so find which one.

*Move:*
$$a_c=\frac{v^{2}}{r}=\omega^{2}r,\qquad F_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{mv^{2}}{r},\qquad P=\frac{2\pi r}{v}=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}$$
Here $P$ is the period and $\omega$ the angular speed. Find the net force toward the centre and set it equal to $mv^{2}/r$. On a flat curve friction supplies it, so the fastest safe speed is $v=\sqrt{\mu_sgr}$.

*Example:* A flat curve has radius $30$ m and $\mu_s=0.60$.
$$v_{\max}=\sqrt{\mu_sgr}=\sqrt{0.60(9.8)(30)}\approx13\ \mathrm{m/s}$$

*Trap:* Adding an outward centrifugal force to the diagram of a body in an inertial frame.

*Check:* Required force grows as $v^{2}$ and falls as $r$ grows.
t2.work-energy:
*When:* A force acts through a distance, or you want a speed and have no time.

*Why:* Net work changes the kinetic energy. This skips the acceleration and the time entirely.

*Move:*
$$W=Fs\cos\theta,\qquad W_{\mathrm{net}}=\Delta K=\tfrac12m\left(v_f^{2}-v_i^{2}\right)$$
Find the work of each force, with the angle between force and displacement. Add them with signs. Set the sum equal to the change in kinetic energy. For a variable force use $\int F\,dx$.

*Example:* A $5.0$ kg body starts from rest. A $40$ N force at $37^\circ$ to the motion acts over $5.0$ m. Use $\cos37^\circ\approx0.80$.
$$W=40(5.0)\cos37^\circ=160\ \mathrm J$$
$$v=\sqrt{\frac{2W}{m}}=\sqrt{\frac{320}{5.0}}=8.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$$

*Trap:* Using the whole force instead of its component along the motion.

*Check:* Positive net work speeds the body up and negative net work slows it.
t2.potential:
*When:* Only conservative forces such as gravity and springs do work, or a force comes from a potential energy.

*Why:* Energy that leaves kinetic form is stored as potential and can come back. The path does not matter, only the end points.

*Move:*
$$K_i+U_i=K_f+U_f,\qquad U_g=mgh,\qquad U_s=\tfrac12kx^{2},\qquad F=-\frac{dU}{dx}$$
Choose a zero for $U$. Write the total energy at the start and at the end. Solve for the unknown speed or height. Turning points are where $K=0$.

*Example:* A spring with $k=120$ N/m is compressed $0.25$ m and launches a $0.30$ kg block along a frictionless floor.
$$\tfrac12(120)(0.25)^{2}=\tfrac12(0.30)v^{2}\ \Rightarrow\ v=5.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$$

*Trap:* Applying conservation when friction or another non-conservative force acts.

*Check:* Kinetic energy is never negative, so $U$ cannot exceed the total energy.
t2.momentum:
*When:* A collision, a brief push, or an isolated system where forces act over a short time.

*Why:* A force acting for a time changes momentum. When the net external force is zero, the total momentum cannot change.

*Move:*
$$\vec p=m\vec v,\qquad \vec J=\int\vec F\,dt=\Delta\vec p,\qquad \sum\vec p_{\mathrm{before}}=\sum\vec p_{\mathrm{after}}$$
Choose a positive direction. Write the momentum before and after with signs. For an impulse, take final minus initial, then divide by the contact time for the average force.

*Example:* A $0.25$ kg ball hits a wall at $14$ m/s and rebounds at $6.0$ m/s. Contact lasts $0.020$ s.
$$\Delta p=0.25\,\big(6.0-(-14)\big)=5.0\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$$
$$F_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{5.0}{0.020}=250\ \mathrm N$$

*Trap:* Dropping the sign of a reversed velocity, which makes the change too small.

*Check:* The impulse points along the change in velocity, here away from the wall.
t2.collisions:
*When:* Two bodies interact over a short time and you want their velocities afterwards.

*Why:* Internal forces cancel in pairs, so momentum survives every collision. Kinetic energy survives only if the bodies bounce perfectly.

*Move:*
$$m_1u_1+m_2u_2=m_1v_1+m_2v_2,\qquad e=\frac{v_2-v_1}{u_1-u_2}$$
Always write the momentum equation. Then add the second condition: $e=1$ for elastic, $e=0$ when the bodies stick. For an elastic hit on a target at rest:
$$v_1=\frac{m_1-m_2}{m_1+m_2}\,u_1,\qquad v_2=\frac{2m_1}{m_1+m_2}\,u_1$$
In a ballistic pendulum, use momentum for the hit, then energy for the rise.

*Example:* A $1.5$ kg cart at $8.0$ m/s hits a $2.5$ kg cart at rest and they stick.
$$v=\frac{1.5(8.0)}{1.5+2.5}=3.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$$
$$\Delta K=\tfrac12(4.0)(3.0)^{2}-\tfrac12(1.5)(8.0)^{2}=-30\ \mathrm J$$

*Trap:* Conserving kinetic energy in an inelastic collision.

*Check:* Kinetic energy after the collision is never larger than before.
t2.com:
*When:* A system of several bodies, or two bodies that attract each other.

*Why:* The centre of mass moves as if all mass sat there and only external forces acted. Internal forces drop out.

*Move:*
$$x_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{\sum m_ix_i}{\sum m_i},\qquad M\vec a_{\mathrm{cm}}=\sum\vec F_{\mathrm{ext}},\qquad \mu=\frac{m_1m_2}{m_1+m_2}$$
Take the mass-weighted average of positions. For two bodies, the relative motion behaves like one body of the reduced mass $\mu$ under their mutual force.

*Example:* A $5.0$ kg mass sits at $x=0$ and a $15$ kg mass at $x=8.0$ m.
$$x_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{5.0(0)+15(8.0)}{20}=6.0\ \mathrm m,\qquad \mu=\frac{5.0(15)}{20}=3.75\ \mathrm{kg}$$

*Trap:* Counting internal forces in $\sum\vec F_{\mathrm{ext}}$.

*Check:* The centre of mass lies between the bodies and nearer the heavier one.
t2.torque-statics:
*When:* A rigid body is held still, or a force may turn it about a pivot.

*Why:* A body stays at rest only if forces and turning effects both balance. A force's turning effect grows with its lever arm.

*Move:*
$$\tau=rF\sin\theta,\qquad \sum\vec F=0,\qquad \sum\tau=0$$
Choose a pivot at an unknown force, so that force drops out. Count torques counterclockwise positive. Solve the torque equation first, then the force equations.

*Example:* A uniform $3.0$ m beam of $12$ kg is hinged at a wall. A vertical rope holds the far end.
$$T\,(3.0)=(12)(9.8)(1.5)\ \Rightarrow\ T=59\ \mathrm N$$

*Trap:* Using the full length instead of the perpendicular distance from the pivot, or forgetting the weight acts at the centre.

*Check:* Any other pivot must give the same answer.
t2.rot-dynamics:
*When:* A body spins, rolls, or feels a torque about an axis.

*Why:* Rotation follows the same law as straight-line motion, with torque in place of force and moment of inertia in place of mass.

*Move:*
$$\tau=I\alpha,\qquad v=\omega R,\qquad K=\tfrac12mv^{2}+\tfrac12I\omega^{2}$$
$$I_{\mathrm{hoop}}=mR^{2},\quad I_{\mathrm{disk}}=\tfrac12mR^{2},\quad I_{\mathrm{sphere}}=\tfrac25mR^{2}$$
Use $I$ about the same axis as the torque. Rolling without slipping means the contact point is at rest, so $v=\omega R$. The rotational share of the energy, with $I=cmR^{2}$, is
$$\frac{K_{\mathrm{rot}}}{K}=\frac{c}{1+c}$$

*Example:* A hoop of mass $3.0$ kg and radius $0.20$ m feels a torque of $0.60$ N m.
$$I=mR^{2}=3.0(0.20)^{2}=0.12\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2},\qquad \alpha=\frac{0.60}{0.12}=5.0\ \mathrm{rad/s^2}$$

*Trap:* Using $mR^{2}$ for every shape, or measuring $I$ about the wrong axis.

*Check:* The larger $I$ is, the smaller the angular acceleration for the same torque.
t2.ang-mom:
*When:* A spinning system changes shape, or collides, with no outside torque about its axis.

*Why:* Angular momentum changes only through an external torque. Pulling mass inward must therefore raise the spin rate.

*Move:*
$$\vec L=\vec r\times\vec p,\qquad L=I\omega=mvr\ \text{(point mass, tangential }v\text{)},\qquad I_1\omega_1=I_2\omega_2$$
Check that the external torque about the axis is zero. Write $L$ before and after. Solve for the new $\omega$. Energy is not conserved here.

*Example:* A skater with $I=6.0$ kg m$^2$ spins at $1.5$ rad/s and pulls in her arms to $I=2.0$ kg m$^2$.
$$\omega_2=\frac{I_1\omega_1}{I_2}=\frac{6.0(1.5)}{2.0}=4.5\ \mathrm{rad/s}$$

*Trap:* Conserving kinetic energy as well. Here it rises from $6.8$ to $20$ J because her arms do work.

*Check:* A smaller $I$ means a faster spin.
t2.gravitation:
*When:* A body orbits, or moves freely under the pull of a large mass.

*Why:* Gravity supplies the inward force of a circular orbit. Setting $GMm/r^{2}$ equal to $mv^{2}/r$ ties speed, radius, and period together, and the satellite mass cancels.

*Move:*
$$F=\frac{GMm}{r^{2}},\qquad v_{\mathrm{orb}}=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}},\qquad v_{\mathrm{esc}}=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}},\qquad T^{2}\propto r^{3}$$
Use $GM_E=3.98\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{m^3/s^2}$ and $R_E=6.37\times10^{6}$ m. At a planet's surface $GM=gR^{2}$, so $g$ falls as $1/r^{2}$ outside. Measure $r$ from the centre of the planet, not from the surface.

*Example:* Find the circular orbital speed at $300$ km altitude.
$$r=6.37\times10^{6}+3.0\times10^{5}=6.67\times10^{6}\ \mathrm m$$
$$v=\sqrt{\frac{3.98\times10^{14}}{6.67\times10^{6}}}\approx7.7\ \mathrm{km/s}$$

*Trap:* Using the altitude as $r$, or taking $\sqrt{GM/R}$ for escape speed. The circular-orbit value is smaller than the escape value.

*Check:* Escape speed is $\sqrt2$ times the circular speed at the same radius.
t2.shm:
*When:* A restoring force grows in proportion to the displacement, as for a spring or a small-angle pendulum.

*Why:* A force $-kx$ gives acceleration $-(k/m)x$, whose solution is a sinusoid with a frequency fixed by $k$ and $m$, not by the amplitude.

*Move:*
$$\omega=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}},\qquad T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega},\qquad v_{\max}=A\omega,\qquad a_{\max}=A\omega^{2},\qquad E=\tfrac12kA^{2}$$
$$\omega_{\mathrm{pendulum}}=\sqrt{\frac{g}{L}}$$
Find $\omega$ from the system. Read the amplitude $A$ from the start. Energy swaps between kinetic and potential.

*Example:* A $0.80$ kg mass on a $20$ N/m spring is pulled $0.15$ m and released.
$$\omega=\sqrt{\frac{20}{0.80}}=5.0\ \mathrm{rad/s},\qquad T=\frac{2\pi}{5.0}=1.26\ \mathrm s$$
$$v_{\max}=0.15(5.0)=0.75\ \mathrm{m/s}$$

*Trap:* Thinking the period depends on amplitude, or putting $g$ into the spring formula.

*Check:* A stiffer spring or a lighter mass gives a shorter period.
t2.damped-driven:
*When:* An oscillator loses energy to friction or drag, or is pushed at some driving frequency.

*Why:* Damping drains the amplitude exponentially. Driving at the natural frequency feeds energy in at the best moment, so the response peaks.

*Move:*
$$x=Ae^{-t/\tau}\cos\omega_dt,\qquad \tau=\frac{2m}{b},\qquad \omega_d=\sqrt{\omega_0^{2}-\left(\frac{b}{2m}\right)^{2}},\qquad Q=\frac{\omega_0m}{b}$$
$$A_{\mathrm{driven}}=\frac{F}{\sqrt{m^{2}(\omega_0^{2}-\omega^{2})^{2}+b^{2}\omega^{2}}},\qquad A_{\mathrm{res}}=\frac{F}{b\,\omega_0}$$
Here $b$ is the damping constant in $F=-bv$, $\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}$, and $F$ and $\omega$ are the amplitude and frequency of the driving force. Energy decays as $e^{-bt/m}$.

*Example:* A $3.0$ kg mass on a $48$ N/m spring has $b=0.60$ kg/s. Find the amplitude fraction after $20$ s, then $Q$, then the resonant amplitude for $F=2.4$ N.
$$\tau=\frac{2m}{b}=10\ \mathrm s,\qquad \frac{A}{A_0}=e^{-20/10}=0.14,\qquad \omega_0=4.0\ \mathrm{rad/s}$$
$$Q=\frac{4.0(3.0)}{0.60}=20,\qquad A_{\mathrm{res}}=\frac{2.4}{0.60(4.0)}=1.0\ \mathrm m$$

*Trap:* Using $m/b$ for the amplitude decay time. That is the decay time of the energy.

*Check:* Amplitude falls by $e$ every $\tau$. Light damping leaves $\omega_d\approx\omega_0$, and $Q=\omega_0\tau/2$.
